blocks.text: 2009 年，Ali Ghodsi 是 UC Berkeley 的访问研究员，他观察互联网公司如何利用海量数据集预测人们会点击、购买和观看什么。那是一个人们频繁谈论“大数据”的时代。当时领先的框架是 Hadoop，Yahoo、Facebook、Twitter 和 LinkedIn 等公司用它在上千台廉价商用服务器上并行处理数据工作负载。在 Hadoop 之前，处理更大工作负载的标准做法是从 Oracle 或 IBM 等厂商购买更大的机器，每台耗资数百万美元，因此 Hadoop 是一个有吸引力的替代方案。

blocks.text: Hadoop 的关键缺陷在于，计算的每一轮都会先把结果保存到磁盘，然后才能开始下一轮。这使得集群中某台廉价机器故障时工作更容易恢复，这是一个合理的选择。但对于机器学习这类迭代式工作负载——做出预测、衡量误差、更新模型，然后重复——它慢得令人痛苦。Hadoop 把每一轮都当作一个新作业，每次都从磁盘重新加载相同的数据，因此集群每花几秒钟改进模型，就要花几分钟搬运数据。

blocks.text: 这个问题促使 Berkeley 的博士生 Matei Zaharia 编写了 Apache Spark 的第一个版本。Spark 建立在 Hadoop 将数据处理工作分散到廉价机器上的创新之上，但让应用在轮次之间把频繁复用的数据保留在服务器快得多的内存中，而不是每次都从磁盘加载——同时不放弃容错能力。这使得这些重复性工作负载快了多达十倍。该实验室于 2010 年将其开源，三年后，Ali、Matei 和另外五位同僚研究者创立了 Databricks，将运行 Spark 所需分布式基础设施的复杂性——集群、扩缩容、安全——抽象到面向企业的单一平台之后。

blocks.text: Spark 加速了数据处理，但数据存放在哪里是另一个问题。那个时代的企业数据占据两个彼此分离的世界。数据仓库保存结构化、可信的记录，让分析师能用 SQL 对其提问，并支撑每一个仪表盘和季度报告。数据湖为其他一切提供廉价存储，比如文档、图像、录音和日志。数据湖很便宜，所以团队把所有东西都倒进去；但进入时没有任何检查或结构化。尽管 TensorFlow 和 PyTorch 等庞大的 AI 开源工具生态围绕数据湖成长起来，但很难从一堆你无法信任的数据中获取价值，这也让它们得了个“数据沼泽”的绰号。

blocks.text: 两个系统各自解决了一个问题，却也制造了一道鸿沟。工程师和数据科学家用 Python 生活在数据湖里，分析师则用 SQL 生活在数据仓库里。每当一方需要另一方的数据时，就得有人搭建管道来搬运。这让公司留下了大量副本、管道、权限和相互冲突的定义。但在 2010 年代后期，Databricks、Uber 和 Netflix 各自独立地得出了同一个解决方案。他们的项目（Delta Lake、Hudi 和 Iceberg）在湖中的文件之上增加了一个表层，赋予其类似数据仓库的保障，例如全有或全无的更新、模式管理和版本化历史。公司不再需要把数据搬进单独的数据仓库来获得可靠性和性能，而是可以直接在数据原本所在的存储上运行仓库式工作负载。正是这一突破让新架构成为可能。

blocks.text: 所以在2025年，Databricks 收购了Neon，这是一家无服务器Postgres公司，其数据库已经主要由AI代理创建，它代表了一种新的数据库架构类别，称为lakebase（这促使Databricks将整合了Neon后形成的产品命名为“Lakebase”）。正如lakehouse在数据湖之上重建了数据仓库，Lakebase将同样的理念应用于操作型数据库。它将存储与计算分离，因此数据可以廉价地存储在数据湖中，而计算则随需求扩展或收缩。而且，由于操作型数据库和lakehouse共享相同的底层存储，数据库的变更会自动对分析师、工程师和代理可用，无需构建和维护错综复杂的管道网络。Databricks将这种事务与分析处理的统一称为LTAP，即Lake Transaction/Analytical Processing。

blocks.text: 他的答案归结为交易成本。找到合适的人、就做什么事以什么价格进行谈判，以及全程监督，都需要时间和金钱。企业用一种更开放式的安排取代了部分重复的市场交易，在这种安排中，管理者在约定范围内调配资源。但在企业内部组织工作也并非没有成本。随着公司成长，更多信息必须经过更多人之手传递，最终，在内部组织下一笔交易的成本会与从市场购买一样高。在科斯的论述中，企业会一直扩张，直到这两种成本相等。

blocks.text: 在智能体化企业中，优秀的人才将比以往任何时候都更有价值。但优秀的人才也会来来去去。与此同时，模型在不断进步，而每个竞争对手都能租用同样的模型。那么，企业究竟如何在这个新世界中建立可持续的竞争优势？

inlines.text: 在智能体化企业中，优秀的人才将比以往任何时候都更有价值。但优秀的人才也会来来去去。与此同时，模型在不断进步，而每个竞争对手都能租用同样的模型。那么，企业究竟如何在这个新世界中建立可持续的竞争优势？

blocks.text: 设想两家银行租用同一个前沿模型来辅助信贷决策。第一家向模型发送提示词，收到答案，并记录最终决策。第二家则记录哪些事实产生了答案、任何人工推翻、哪些决策表现良好、哪些失败，并全程调整其策略。一年后，当更好的模型出现时，只有其中一家建成了更好的银行。如果你更换公司的 AI 模型，而新模型继承了你的定义、权限、已评估案例、客户历史和来之不易的例外情况，那就是可持续竞争优势的基础。如果新 AI 模型与其他人从同样的提示词起步，那就不是。

blocks.text: Databricks has recently been described as “a data company that caught the AI wave.” But the company was built by AI researchers a decade before the wave arrived. The business is four technology S-curves stacked over nearly two decades – Spark, Lakehouse, Lakebase, and now agents – each of which created the innovation window for the next. blocks.text: In 2009, Ali Ghodsi was a visiting researcher at UC Berkeley watching internet companies use enormous datasets to predict what people would click, buy, and watch. This was a time when people talked about “Big Data” a lot. The leading framework was Hadoop, which companies like Yahoo, Facebook, Twitter, and LinkedIn used to process data workloads in parallel across thousands of cheap, commodity servers. Before Hadoop, the standard way to process larger workloads was to buy a bigger machine from vendors like Oracle or IBM that cost millions of dollars each, so Hadoop was an attractive alternative.

blocks.text: Hadoop’s critical flaw was that each round of a computation saved its results to disk before the next could begin. That made work easier to recover when one of the cluster’s cheap machines failed, which was a sensible choice. But it was painfully slow for iterative workloads like machine learning, where you make predictions, measure the error, update a model, and then repeat. Hadoop treated each round as a new job and reloaded the same data from disk every time, so the cluster spent minutes moving data for every few seconds of improving the model.

blocks.text: This problem inspired Matei Zaharia, a PhD student at Berkeley, to write the first version of Apache Spark. Spark built on Hadoop’s innovation of spreading data processing work across cheap machines, but let applications keep frequently reused data in the servers’ much faster memory between rounds instead of loading it from disk each time – without giving up fault tolerance. That made these repetitive workloads up to ten times faster. The lab open-sourced it in 2010, and three years later, Ali, Matei, and five of their fellow researchers founded Databricks to abstract away the complexity of running the distributed infrastructure Spark required – the clusters, the scaling, the security – behind a single platform for the enterprise.

blocks.text: Spark sped up data processing, but where that data lived was another problem. Enterprise data in that era occupied two separate worlds. Data warehouses held the structured, trustworthy records that let analysts ask questions of them in SQL and powered every dashboard and quarterly report. Data lakes provided cheap storage for everything else, like documents, images, recordings, and logs. Data lakes were cheap, so teams dumped everything into them; but nothing was checked or structured on the way in. Even though a vast ecosystem of AI open-source tools like TensorFlow and PyTorch grew around the data lake, it was hard to get value from a pile of data you couldn’t trust, which earned them the nickname “data swamps.”

blocks.text: Both systems solved a problem, but they created a divide. Engineers and data scientists lived in the lake with Python while analysts lived in the warehouse with SQL. Whenever one side needed the other’s data, someone had to build a pipeline to move it. This left the company with lots of copies, pipelines, permissions, and conflicting definitions. But in the late 2010s, Databricks, Uber, and Netflix each landed on the same fix independently. Their projects (Delta Lake, Hudi, and Iceberg) added a table layer over the files in the lake, giving them warehouse-like guarantees such as all-or-nothing updates, schema management, and versioned history. Instead of moving the data into a separate warehouse for reliability and performance, a company could now run warehouse-style workloads on the same storage where the data already lived. It was the breakthrough that made a new architecture possible.

blocks.text: In 2020, Databricks invented the “lakehouse” by merging the data lake and the data warehouse. It combined the cheap, flexible storage of the data lake with the strict reliability and fast query performance of a data warehouse, then made warehouse-grade SQL and machine learning first-class workloads on the same foundation. The cheap storage that held everything became trustworthy enough to serve as the data foundation that engineers, data scientists, and data analysts could finally share. “The best data warehouse is a lakehouse,” went the tagline, and customers seemed to agree. Today, Databricks’ Lakehouse runs at a more than $1.5 billion revenue run-rate, growing over 100% year over year.

The lake was also a powerful foundation for machine learning and AI, which, Vogels wrote, “thrive on large, diverse datasets.”

The operational database, which manages real-time transactions for day-to-day business operations, like processing payments or user logins, was still stitched to the lakehouse by a web of fragile pipelines. Compute and storage remained bundled in one monolithic box, and data was trapped in proprietary formats that made migrations one of the scariest technical projects in any organization.

blocks.text: So in 2025, Databricks bought Neon, a serverless Postgres company whose databases were already being created mostly by AI agents, and which represented a new architectural category of databases, called lakebase (inspiring Databricks to call the resulting product that integrated Neon into Databricks “Lakebase”). Just as the lakehouse rebuilt the warehouse on top of the data lake, Lakebase applies the same idea to the operational database. It separates storage from compute so data can be stored cheaply in the data lake while compute scales up or down with demand. And because operational databases and the lakehouse share the same underlying storage, database changes automatically become available to analysts, engineers, and agents, without a web of pipelines to build and maintain. Databricks calls this unification of transactions and analytics LTAP, for Lake Transaction/Analytical Processing.

blocks.text: Every company has an ontology – a working model of what exists, how those things relate, what its words mean, and which source governs when two disagree. Parts of it live in databases, dashboards, policies, and documents. But much of it lives only in the heads of experienced employees. It’s also never finished. Contracts change, workarounds become processes, exceptions become rules, and the official record drifts away from how the work is actually done. The same is true of who decides what and of remembering which decisions were right – authority and evaluation are just as unwritten as ontology. People compensate for all of it almost invisibly. inlines.text: The Nature of the Firm

blocks.text: In his 1937 article “The Nature of the Firm,” economist Ronald Coase asked why firms exist at all. If markets can coordinate activity through prices and contracts, why bring people together inside companies and subject their work to managerial direction?

The Nature of the Firm

blocks.text: His answer came down to transaction costs. Finding the right person, negotiating what needs to be done at what price, and monitoring it all take time and money. A firm replaces some of those repeated market transactions with a more open-ended arrangement in which managers direct resources within agreed limits. But organizing work inside a firm is not free either. As a company grows, more information has to travel through more people, and eventually, the cost of organizing the next transaction internally costs as much as buying it from the market. In Coase’s account, the firm expands until those two costs meet.
